articles.title: Thune: Ads promoting Trump political message ‘shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars’
articles.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday that while he likes President Trump’s new ads pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” they “shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars.” Thune warned Trump about using taxpayer money for ads that resemble the political ads he ran online during the 2024 presidential…
articles.body:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday that while he likes President Trump’s new ads pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists,” they “shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars.”

Thune warned Trump about using taxpayer money for ads that resemble the political ads he ran online during the 2024 presidential campaign.

“It’s a great message. I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Thune said Monday afternoon as he walked into the Capitol.

The new ad, which ran on television over the weekend , airing during “Fox News Sunday” and several NFL and college football games, is part of a series of ads with the disclaimer: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

It is nearly identical to an online ad he posted to his Truth Social account in January 2024, when he was revving up his victorious campaign for president, which urged supporters to text “TRUMP to 88022” to support his campaign.

The latest iteration of the ad, however, ends with a disclaimer informing viewers that it was “paid for by the U.S. government.”

Richard Painter, a White House ethics lawyer under then-President George W. Bush, posted on social platform X that the use of taxpayer money to promote the president’s political message ahead of the midterm elections “ could be an impeachable offense .”

Common Cause, the good-government advocacy group, issued a statement warning that “running political messaging stamped with ‘Paid for by the U.S. Government’ dangerously crosses the line from public service to authoritarian self-promotion.”

The White House has defended the clips, arguing in a statement that they “are clearly not campaign ads” because Trump is not up for reelection this November.

“The announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad. That’s not partisanship — that’s a government that still believes in the country it serves,” the White House said in its statement.

articles.title: New polls have Democrats thinking big on Senate
articles.summary: Recent polling showing Democrats performing strongly in Senate battlegrounds and more reliably red states is fueling optimism that the party could clinch both chambers in November. An AARP poll released Monday showed Democrat Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley by 11 percentage points in the North Carolina Senate race, while recent polls have shown…
articles.body:
Recent polling showing Democrats performing strongly in Senate battlegrounds and more reliably red states is fueling optimism that the party could clinch both chambers in November.

An AARP poll released Monday showed Democrat Roy Cooper leading Republican Michael Whatley by 11 percentage points in the North Carolina Senate race, while recent polls have shown Democrat James Talarico tied or leading Republican Ken Paxton in Texas.

Republicans have a few opportunities to expand their own map in Michigan, New Hampshire and potentially Minnesota. But the Senate is clearly in play for Democrats — which analysts like Charlie Cook note seemed almost impossible a year ago “but now it’s very realistic.”

“I don’t feel good about the election as a Republican,” said Brian Darling, a former top aide to Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.). “I think it’s going to be a bad day.”

Most election forecasters and analysts expect Democrats to win back the House in November by varying margins, while a handful now predict a rosier environment for the upper chamber.

Inside Elections and Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) suggest Democrats could very well flip the Senate, which would require picking up at least four seats. Inside Elections projects Democrats will take between two and four seats in the Senate while DDHQ forecasts that the party has a 54 percent chance of winning the upper chamber.

Cook, the founder of the nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report, suggested in a weekend interview with ABC News’s “This Week” that Democrats could pick up 20 seats in the House and between four and five in the Senate.

“I would completely agree that the House has been kind of a done deal for a good while,” Cook said. “But the Senate, a year ago, it wasn’t realistic to think that the Senate might flip.”

The increasing optimism for Democrats comes amid rising voter anger over the economy as well as the Trump administration’s war in Iran. The party holds an 11-point lead over Republicans on the general congressional ballot, per the latest Emerson College Polling survey.

And, with the House out of session until after the election and the Senate in town for just a few more days, some strategists suggest it falls on President Trump to turn the tides for his party before Nov. 3.

“If a deal was cut on the Iran war, and if there was an actual winding down and an end game that was presented to the American people, I think that would be very helpful to Republicans,” Darling said.

“I think that is the one issue that would move a lot of voters back over into the Republican fold.”

But with no end of the war in sight before the midterms, polling suggests a favorable outcome for Democrats is likely, even as experts acknowledge it’s an imperfect science.

A Texas Public Opinion Research poll released on Friday showed Talarico leading Paxton by 5 points, just outside the survey’s margin of error. Talarico also handily led Paxton among independents — 58 percent to 26 percent, respectively.

A recent Marist poll also showed Talarico leading Paxton by 6 points — 50 percent to 44 percent, respectively. Some polling also has Talarico slightly ahead by a point or tied.

A separate Marist poll had Democrat Josh Turek polling ahead of Republican Ashley Hinson by 8 points in the Iowa Senate race.

While the Iowa Senate race is expected to be much tighter, the Republican-leaning pollster Trafalgar Group suggested in a recent survey that Hinson only edged Turek out by 2 points — while separately forecasting GOP Sen. Darline Graham (S.C.) polling within the margin of error against Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina.

The last time Iowa was represented by a Democrat in the Senate was 18 years ago, while South Carolina hasn’t elected a member of the party to the upper chamber since 1998.

“Republicans’ scandal-plagued candidates are facing backlash for making everything cost more — and Democrats are well-positioned to flip seats and win the majority,” said Maeve Coyle, a spokesperson for the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm.

Steve Jarding, a longtime Democratic strategist who’s worked on Senate campaigns, estimated the party could win between six and seven seats in the fall. Unless the GOP injects an influx of cash into all the competitive races, Jarding suggested, it’s increasingly unlikely Republicans will narrow the gap.

“If you’re the party in power, and your message isn’t working for you, it’s almost too late by June. But certainly, you get into the first of October where we’re at— it’s almost impossible to change that narrative,” Jarding said.

Other Republicans are inclined to put less stock into the polls after a pair of surveys were off base in Democratic primaries in Wisconsin and Michigan this summer.

“Democrats should think twice before relying too heavily on the same rosy polling that grossly overestimated socialist Abdul El-Sayed in last month’s Michigan primary,” said Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm.

But Republican pollster Whit Ayres suggested Senate control remains up in the air with as many as 12 seats in play.

“It’s overwhelmingly the increase in inflation and an economy that can’t seem to get going that has created an environment that’s favorable for the party out of power at the moment,” he said.

One bright spot for Republicans is its immense cash advantage over Democrats. Recent figures from ad-tracking firm AdImpact show the GOP spending more in future ad reservations in eight of nine competitive Senate elections. Democrats narrowly edge out Republicans in North Carolina.

The GOP is also in a position to benefit from a recent Supreme Court ruling paving the way for campaigns and state parties to coordinate and spend unlimited amounts of money.

Still, the overwhelmingly negative polling for the GOP is impossible to ignore.

“Republicans can look at the fact that the polling is an inexact science, and it could be pretty far off,” Darling said. “But notwithstanding that, it still doesn’t look great because the polls have been overwhelmingly bad news for Republicans.”

articles.title: Vance, RFK Jr., Mike Tyson to speak at MAHA Summit in DC
articles.summary: Vice President Vance, Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and former boxing heavyweight Mike Tyson are slated to speak Tuesday for the second Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Summit in Washington, D.C. The event will conclude with a “fireside chat” between Vance and Kennedy, the summit’s agenda online shows. Organizers told…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance, Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and former boxing heavyweight Mike Tyson are slated to speak Tuesday for the second Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Summit in Washington, D.C.

The event will conclude with a “fireside chat” between Vance and Kennedy, the summit’s agenda online shows . Organizers told Politico that the discussion will be “about MAHA’s accomplishments, its regulatory reform agenda and its priorities for the year ahead.”

“Since January 2025, thanks to the work of @SecKennedy and the team over at @HHSGov, we have been fulfilling that promise to the American people, and the great MAHA movement,” Vance wrote Monday on the social platform X . “Tune in tomorrow to hear more about the great work being done, and what is coming in the future to secure a stronger nation full of healthier Americans.”

Kennedy’s wife, “Curb Your Enthusiasm” star Cheryl Hines, will precede her husband and the vice president to deliver an “exciting announcement,” according to the agenda.

Tyson will take part in a panel about the “MAHA athlete,” having appeared in a Super Bowl ad earlier this year promoting the MAHA campaign and urging people to eat “real food.” Last year’s speakers for this portion of the summit featured former NASCAR driver Danica Patrick, UFC President Dana White and Russell Cook, the co-founder and president of fitness app FitOn.

The boxer has been a longtime friend of President Trump since the 1980s. As a businessman, Trump served as Tyson’s business adviser and later defended the boxer before and after he was convicted of rape in 1992. Trump later appeared among several celebrities at Tyson’s first fight after he was released from prison — against Peter McNeeley in 1995.

Other speakers set to appear at the summit include comedian Russell Brand, who will moderate a discussion with U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Mehmet Oz and HHS chief counselor Chris Klomp about reforms made to the CMS. Brand has been a supporter of the MAHA campaign, Politico reported.

Brand is set to go to trial next month in the United Kingdom on several charges of rape and sexual assault . The comedian has denied any wrongdoing.

Cabinet members joining to speak include Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin. Rollins will be part of a “fireside chat” with Ohalo Genetics CEO David Friedberg about “securing America’s food supply and environmental innovation,” while Zeldin will be part of a panel moderated by summit organizer Tony Lyons about “modernizing MAHA regulation.”

Walmart Senior Vice President Scott Morris, Sweetgreen CEO Jonathan Neman and chief MAHA officer at Steak ‘n Shake Michael Boes will be part of a talk on “real food at scale” moderated by HHS deputy chief of staff Stefanie Spear. Boes previously worked as a senior HHS adviser before joining Steak ‘n Shake.

Walmart is one of the summit’s sponsors, along with Anthropic, OpenAI, Noom, Hims & Hers, Helus Pharma and Wild Alaskan Company, among others.

The event is intended to show the MAHA movement’s changes to food and health safety in the U.S. ahead of the November midterm elections, which could have an impact on Kennedy’s agenda at the HHS.

Lyons has asked MAHA campaign members to vote Republican in November to prevent Kennedy from appearing before Democratic-controlled hearings should the party reclaim either chamber of Congress after the midterms, according to Politico.

Trump has had Kennedy appear on the campaign trail in key battleground House districts to promote the MAHA agenda. The president will be able to prioritize more of Kennedy’s agenda should the MAHA coalition become a reliable conservative voting bloc in November.

articles.title: Shaheen presses Senate to cap insulin costs
articles.summary: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare The Big Story Shaheen makes last-minute insulin pitch Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) is pressing Senate leadership to hold a floor vote on bipartisan legislation to cap insulin costs in private insurance before lawmakers leave town until after the midterm election. © Greg Nash…
articles.body:
Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) is pressing Senate leadership to hold a floor vote on bipartisan legislation to cap insulin costs in private insurance before lawmakers leave town until after the midterm election.

“President Trump campaigned on immediately lowering costs for the American people, yet he’s done just the opposite. With millions of American families facing spiking prices as a result of this Administration’s disastrous health care policies, my INSULIN Act is one immediate step Congress can take to directly lower costs for millions of Americans,” Shaheen said in a statement Monday.

The veteran lawmaker is retiring and wants to get the legislation across the finish line before the end of the year. Shaheen has also personally spoken to the White House about the measure, and staff-level conversations have been ongoing since, according to a Democratic aide.

The legislation would out-of-pocket costs for insulin at $35 for people with commercial insurance, expanding a cap for people on Medicare that passed in President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. It would also create a pilot program in 10 states to cap costs for uninsured people.

The bill, which is led by Shaheen, Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) and John Kennedy (R-La.). passed the Senate Health Education, Labor and Pensions Committee by a vote of 17-5 in July . In total, it has 28 co-sponsors divided equally between the parties — meaning there are 60 votes in the Senate if all Democrats vote for it.

While the effort likely won’t yield a vote this week, the most likely path forward would be including the measure as part of a year-end spending bill. Discussions are also happening about attaching the measure to the must-pass defense policy and spending authorization bill.

A bipartisan House version was introduced earlier this month by Reps. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Angie Craig (D-Minn.), Kim Schrier (D-Wash.), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa) and Rob Bresnahan (R-Pa.). Miller-Meeks and Bresnahan face competitive reelection races.

There’s no guarantee the measure will pass. Lawmakers have discussed the idea of an insulin cap for years but haven’t been able to get legislation over the finish line over GOP resistance to government setting prices.

Notably, HELP committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) voted against the bill, arguing it created an unnecessary and duplicative government grant program.

Cassidy noted many community health centers already provide deeply discounted insulin to patients who need it and criticized the federal drug pricing program that he says hospitals are abusing.

articles.title: Hegseth instructs Pentagon to defend 2026 elections from ‘foreign actors’
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth instructed the Pentagon last week to prioritize and deploy “advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities” to track down, disru...
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth instructed the Pentagon last week to prioritize and deploy "advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities" to track down, disrupt and neutralize "foreign actors to protect the 2026 midterm elections" while "maintaining the fundamental freedoms that characterize our country."

"Commander U.S. Cyber Command and the Directors of the Combat Support Agencies will prioritize the use of DoW [Department of War] intelligence and cyber capabilities to ensure foreign actors do not meddle in our democratic systems," Hegseth said in a Sept. 22 memo , which was made public Monday.

The Pentagon chief directed the Defense Intelligence Enterprise to execute collection and production on foreign threats to U.S. elections in accordance with the "law, regulation, Executive direction and DoW policies and directives."

Hegseth instructed Gen. Joshua Rudd, head of U.S. Cyber Command, to use existing capabilities and authorities in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security to counter "potential cyber threats from foreign actors targeting our elections."

"Our Nation's ability to conduct free and fair elections is a steadfast principal of our Democracy," Hegseth said in the one-page memo. "Assuring and protecting this ability is a no-fail mission and the DoW will do its part in supporting this whole of government effort."

The meddling of foreign actors and nations has been a concern for U.S. administrations.

Similarly, in 2022, the National Security Agency (NSA) and U.S. Cyber Command under former President Biden highlighted a similar push to safeguard the 2022 midterms from foreign interference and influence.

Rudd told senators during a hearing in January that he would work on safeguarding U.S. elections and protect from foreign interference.

"U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency are closely partnered to identify and defend against cyber threats to our nation. The Command and the Agency regularly counter actions by malicious foreign cyber actors including those with the intent to interfere with our democratic process," Rudd said in a statement Monday.

articles.title: As Republicans break with Trump, one gets a brushback: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, senior national political reporter Sahil Kapur looks at how Trump is reacting to Republicans putting some distance between themselves and the White House before the midterms. Plus, senior reporter Alexander Smith digs into a big issue in European politics with some echoes in recent U.S. politics — links between domestic right-wing parties and Russia. — Scott Bland As Republicans break with Trump, one gets a brushback Analysis by Sahil Kapur With President Donald Trump‘s approval rating dipping and voters turning toward Democrats ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, numerous Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him — scrubbing him from their websites, using their voices or votes to disapprove of the Iran war, and more. For the most part, Trump has let it slide, in some cases downplaying the political signaling by wary allies to his skeptics in the electorate. But not in the case of Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, the three-term Florida Republican who represents a Miami-area district. Last week, she ran a straight-to-camera ad, filmed outside the White House, condemning Trump’s immigration agenda. “Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she says in the ad, pointing at the camera and adding that “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Salazar has reason to be worried, even though she won her last two elections by double digits and Trump handily carried her district in 2024. The district is 74% Hispanic. Between 2020 and 2024, Trump made double-digit gains with Hispanic voters nationwide, according to exit polls. But his ratings have fallen precipitously since then. In the latest NBC News poll, Latino voters disapproved of Trump by 2 to 1. Other Republicans have cause for concern, too. Trump’s national approval rating is 39% in the NBC News polling average (or about 20 points underwater), falling from 50% (or about 5 points above water) when his second term began. Against that backdrop, Republican candidates have sought some distance on Iran, gas prices and other issues in recent weeks. But it was Salazar who faced the brunt of Trump’s ire. Over the weekend, the president went on Truth Social to repost more than a dozen social media posts slamming Salazar. “She’s openly pro-amnesty,” said one commenter reposted by Trump. “She tried a stunt and it backfired!” wrote another. “She is nothing but a back stabber,” wrote yet another. “Trump must remove his endorsement from her,” said a fourth. A fifth commenter boosted by Trump called for replacing her with a “new” Republican. It serves as a warning shot to other Republicans not to cross the line or he’ll put them on blast with his base of supporters, whom the GOP needs to turn out to vote in November. Less clear is where the line is. Salazar’s direct and public confrontation on TV — which has long been Trump’s preferred media — ran afoul of it. But Florida governor candidate Byron Donalds, who has removed mentions of Trump from his website, did not violate his red line; Trump downplayed his distancing on social media. Neither did Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who voted two weeks ago for a Democratic-led resolution to end the Iran war, or Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who last week said the war should end. On Monday, Trump hosted Iowa lawmakers, including Miller-Meeks and Hinson, in the Oval Office to announce a new steel plant in Iowa. “We’re going to do a great rally. We’ll all be there together. We have to get you all elected,” Trump said. “We’ll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir,” Hinson chimed in. Does Europe’s far right have a Kremlin problem? By Alexander Smith Europe’s far-right parties are on the rise, seemingly well positioned to ride a groundswell of anti-establishment sentiment into power in several countries in the next few years. But as anxiety mounts over threats of sabotage and cyberattacks from Russia, the resurgent right is facing scrutiny over past ties to the Kremlin — and questions about how it might approach Moscow in the future. A striking pivot came this month from French far-right figurehead Marine Le Pen, the front-runner in next year’s presidential election. In a joint statement with Jordan Bardella, another key figure within her National Rally party, Le Pen said she would “never tolerate” Russia using “intimidation, threats, destabilization or psychological pressure” to influence French policy. They also condemned Moscow’s seizure of French and other European companies’ assets as “a hostile act against the interests of France and the nations of Europe” that “must be firmly condemned.” It’s a notable rhetorical evolution from Le Pen, who only a few years ago was declaring her admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin, playing down threats from Moscow and facing intense scrutiny over a 9.4 million-euro ($10.7 million) loan to her party from a Russian bank. Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Scott Bland. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Trump CMS faces bipartisan pushback over Medicare proposal tied to Biden-era drug pricing law
articles.summary: Lawmakers say the proposed Medicare policy could make it harder for patients to access newer cancer treatments by discouraging medical innovation.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A bipartisan group of more than 50 lawmakers is urging the Trump administration not to finalize a proposed Medicare policy tied to the Biden-era drug price negotiation program, arguing it could discourage development of improved cancer treatments. In a Sept. 21 letter obtained by Fox News Digital, the lawmakers called on Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz to remove the agency's proposed fixed-dose combination policy from its final rule implementing Medicare's Drug Price Negotiation Program. The Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program was created under the Inflation Reduction Act, which former President Joe Biden signed into law in 2022. The Trump administration proposed the policy in June as part of implementing that program. At the center of the dispute is how Medicare would treat newer versions of existing drugs for price negotiation purposes. DR OZ WARNS MEDICARE SCAMMERS ARE STEALING BILLIONS — AND YOUR PERSONAL INFORMATION COULD BE NEXT The lawmakers argue the proposal would cause some improved treatments to face Medicare price negotiations much sooner after receiving Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval. They say that would reduce incentives for drugmakers to develop better versions of existing medicines. "If finalized, the proposed fixed-dose combination policy would subject these advancements to negotiation almost immediately after FDA approval, harming patient access as well as incentives to develop these improved therapies," the lawmakers wrote. CMS, meanwhile, said the proposal is designed to prevent drugmakers from avoiding or delaying negotiated Medicare prices by making only limited changes to existing drugs and introducing them as new products. DR OZ NAMES 5 STATES IN FRAUD CRACKDOWN AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TARGETS MEDICAID ABUSE The lawmakers pointed to advances in cancer immunotherapy that allow some patients to receive a quick injection instead of spending hours receiving an intravenous infusion. They said those improvements can make treatment faster, easier and more accessible, particularly for patients in rural areas. "Patients fighting cancer deserve access to the most advanced new therapies, and if CMS finalizes this proposal, those advances are less likely to reach those who need it the most," the letter states. The lawmakers also argued the FDA already evaluates the therapies as separate medicines, requiring separate clinical trials and approvals. They said CMS should treat those therapies as separate medicines under the Medicare drug price negotiation program. The lawmakers also argued that CMS actuaries "have not been able to show this policy would produce meaningful savings for taxpayers." DR OZ REVEALS THE HEALTHY RETIREMENT HABIT THAT COULD MAKE AMERICA $1 TRILLION RICHER "We strongly urge CMS to withdraw the fixed-dose combination proposal from the final rule," the letter states. "The patients we represent need policies that expand access to lifesaving care and reward medical progress and innovation in the treatment of deadly diseases." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The letter was signed by more than 50 lawmakers from both parties, including Reps. John Joyce, R-Pa., Darin LaHood, R-Ill., Mike Kennedy, R-Utah, Tim Moore, R-N.C., Jim Costa, D-Calif., Donald Davis, D-N.C., and more. CMS could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.

articles.title: Chuck Grassley, oldest sitting senator, laments dying in office under a Dem governor
articles.summary: "I don't want a Democrat governor choosing my successor," Grassley said.
articles.body:
Iowa Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley, the oldest sitting U.S. senator, lamented the possibility that a Democratic governor could appoint his successor if he were to die in office, according to video of remarks he delivered late last week.

"At 93 years of age, I don't know how many more groups of Republicans like this I'm going to have a chance to talk to," Grassley said on Friday during the GOP's annual Reagan Dinner in West Des Moines. "But I want to take advantage of it. But one of the reasons I'm worried about who's going to be elected governor -- I don't plan on dying in office -- but if I did, I don't want a Democrat governor choosing my successor."

Grassley, who celebrated his 93rd birthday on Sept. 17, is currently serving in his eighth term in the Senate -- set to expire Jan. 3, 2029. If Grassley were to die in the next two years, the next governor of Iowa -- set to be elected this fall -- would make a temporary appointment to fill the seat until the 2028 election.

A late June Fox News poll found Democrat Rob Sand, Iowa's state auditor, with a 9-point lead over Republican Zach Lahn among registered voters in the state. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted around the same time found a much closer contest with the candidates essentially neck-and-neck among likely voters.

Grassley has not announced whether he will seek a ninth term in the Senate in 2028.

Discussões sobre candidatos e eleições chegam a escritórios, fábricas e grupos corporativos de WhatsApp. Mas lei proíbe que relações de trabalho sejam usadas para interferir no voto alheio.

A condenação recente de uma empresa por assédio eleitoral chama atenção para uma discussão entre trabalhadores e empregadores que ganha espaço às vésperas das eleições de 2026: até onde vai a liberdade de expressão política e a partir de que ponto uma conduta passa a configurar assédio eleitoral?

Em 4 de setembro, a Justiça trabalhista confirmou que a rede Marabraz terá de pagar indenização de R$ 10 mil a um ex-funcionário por um episódio ocorrido na campanha eleitoral de 2022.

De acordo com a denúncia, a empresa criou um grupo de WhatsApp com funcionários, impediu que eles deixassem a conversa e os submeteu a pressão psicológica para votar no candidato apoiado pela chefia.

A situação entre o ex-funcionário e a empresa teria se agravado após ele questionar o sistema de pagamento de comissões e culminou com a demissão por justa causa em janeiro de 2024.

A Justiça trabalhista, porém, considerou a demissão inválida e a converteu em desligamento sem justa causa. A empresa foi condenada ao pagamento de verbas trabalhistas, comissões descontadas e horas extras, além da indenização por assédio eleitoral.

A Marabraz chegou a recorrer e conseguiu a anulação da primeira sentença, com a realização de nova audiência para ouvir uma testemunha. Mas como a empresa não compareceu à nova sessão, a Justiça manteve as condenações e ainda aplicou multa de 7% sobre o valor da causa por litigância de má-fé.

🔎Ligigância de má-fé é uma atitude desonesta ou abusiva de uma das partes de um processo na Justiça.

Procurada pela DW, a empresa de móveis não quis comentar a decisão judicial.

Em época de campanha, tem sido cada vez mais comum que conversas sobre candidatos, partidos e propostas de governo façam parte do cotidiano do trabalho, seja em conversas de corredor, em grupos de WhatsApp corporativos ou reuniões internas.

O problema, segundo especialistas ouvidos pela DW, começa quando a discussão deixa de ser uma manifestação espontânea e passa a envolver pressão , constrangimento ou tentativa de interferir na escolha política de outra pessoa .

A regra está prevista na Resolução nº 23.755, de março deste ano, que alterou algumas normas sobre propaganda eleitoral. Segundo o texto, quem der causa ou permitir a ocorrência do assédio eleitoral pode responder de acordo com a legislação.

Onde termina a conversa e começa o assédio?

Quando existe dependência econômica ou hierarquia, uma manifestação aparentemente política pode ser interpretada de outra maneira caso esteja associada a ameaças, benefícios, punições ou constrangimentos.

Um comentário feito entre dois colegas, por exemplo, ocorre em condições diferentes de uma orientação dada por um chefe a um funcionário ou pela própria estrutura empresarial.

Entre 2023 e agosto de 2026, a Justiça do Trabalho contabilizou 738 processos relacionados a assédio em ambiente de trabalho, a maioria movida pelos próprios trabalhadores.

Em 92% dos casos analisados, havia características de assédio institucional, ou seja, a pressão política estava ligada à estrutura da empresa e não apenas à atitude isolada de um chefe.

Quase 82% dos casos envolviam o chamado terror psicológico , que é caracterizado por associar a vitória de determinado candidato a demissões, fechamento da empresa ou crise econômica, enquanto o uso de ferramentas digitais, principalmente o WhatsApp, estiveram presentes em mais de 67% das situações.

Os dados são de uma pesquisa realizada pelo Centro de Pesquisas Judiciárias do Conselho Superior da Justiça do Trabalho (CSJT) e do Tribunal Superior do Trabalho (TST).

O Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT) afirma que o assédio eleitoral pode ocorrer tanto presencialmente quanto por meios virtuais e não depende necessariamente de uma sequência de episódios.

Assim, um único ato pode ser suficiente para caracterizar a prática, dependendo das circunstâncias.

A legislação eleitoral não transforma o local de trabalho em um espaço livre de opiniões políticas. Funcionários continuam podendo conversar sobre candidatos e propostas, desde que a manifestação não se transforme em pressão ou propaganda eleitoral irregular dentro da relação profissional.

A principal diferença está na liberdade de quem participa da conversa. Uma discussão entre colegas pode fazer parte da convivência profissional quando todos têm condições de concordar, discordar ou simplesmente deixar o assunto de lado sem medo de consequências.

Essa situação muda quando há uma relação hierárquica e dependência econômica, fator que coloca o trabalhador em uma posição de maior vulnerabilidade.

Um gerente pode ter suas próprias preferências políticas, assim como qualquer trabalhador, mas isso não significa que possa usar sua posição para induzir subordinados a votar em determinado candidato.

"Não é necessário haver ameaça explícita. Sutilezas dentro de uma conversa sugerindo posicionamento político e respostas, isso também pode se configurar um assédio", explica o advogado Marcus Linhares, Head de Gestão e Compliance Trabalhista.

"A linha está entre o diálogo e o constrangimento. A partir do momento em que se constrange por posições políticas já começa a se configurar um assédio eleitoral."

Chefe pode pedir voto para um candidato?

"O chefe pode fazer a sua manifestação pessoal, porque a todos é garantido a expressão livre do pensamento e de suas preferências político-partidárias. Contudo, o limite aparece quando essa preferência passa de mera conversa e começa a se traduzir em interferência no trabalho dos funcionários ", explica Izabelle Paes Omena de Oliveira Lima, especialista em direito eleitoral.

Em outras palavras: um superior não pode usar da sua posição para pressionar funcionários a votar em determinado candidato ou partido.

A situação pode assumir diferentes formas. Uma ameaça explícita, como associar a permanência no emprego ao apoio a um candidato, é uma forma evidente de pressão.

Mas o assédio também pode ser mais sutil, por exemplo quando o empregador deixa claro que espera determinado comportamento político dos funcionários ou sugere que quem não acompanhar sua preferência poderá sofrer algum tipo de consequência profissional.

Também podem entrar nesse contexto promessas de benefícios condicionadas ao voto, ameaças de demissão, mudanças desfavoráveis de escala, redução de oportunidades ou outras formas de prejuízo relacionadas à escolha eleitoral.

"Aquele que exerce a chefia num ambiente de trabalho também tem o direito e a liberdade de manifestar as suas opções políticas.

O que não pode é utilizar da sua função para querer discriminar, trazer qualquer tipo de empecilho ao subordinado, à sua equipe em relação a alguma imposição, algum tipo de sanção ou perseguição ", acrescenta diz Flávio Bernardes, especialista em direito eleitoral e ex-juiz do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral.

O MPT cita ainda como exemplos de possíveis práticas de assédio eleitoral impedir ou dificultar o exercício do voto, descontar do salário o período utilizado para votar ou exigir que esse tempo seja compensado.

Também pode configurar irregularidade definir escalas ou locais de trabalho com o objetivo de facilitar o voto de apoiadores e dificultar o de outros trabalhadores.

Mas não é só o empregador que pode ter sua conduta enquadrada como assédio eleitoral . Isso vale também para colegas, dependendo do contexto, principalmente em discussões que envolvem coação, humilhação, discriminação ou tentativa de manipular a escolha política de outra pessoa.

A análise considera a relação entre os envolvidos e as circunstâncias do episódio.

"A linha sempre vai estar no respeito entre os colegas. A todos é garantido o direito de expressar sua opinião, inclusive política. Todavia, quando essa manifestação deixa de ser uma conversa e passa a ser uma pressão e humilhação ao colega, essa situação pode vir a caracterizar um assédio eleitoral", acrescenta Lima.

O ambiente de trabalho não pode ser transformado em espaço de campanha eleitoral por iniciativa do empregador.

Isso vale para diferentes formatos, como convocar funcionários para participar de uma manifestação política, pedir que compareçam a um evento de campanha ou utilizar canais corporativos para promover determinado candidato.

A conduta pode ultrapassar o limite da liberdade de expressão quando a iniciativa parte da empresa e está vinculada à relação profissional.

A situação torna-se ainda mais sensível quando existe alguma forma de obrigação ou expectativa de participação. Um funcionário que acredita que sua presença pode influenciar sua avaliação, salário, uma promoção ou sua permanência no emprego não está diante de uma manifestação política em condições de igualdade.

"Dentro do ambiente empresarial não se deve realizar manifestações específicas em relação a este ou aquele candidato convidando, especialmente, por parte da direção, toda a equipe e os seus subordinados.

Já há jurisprudência, decisões que colocam que isso pode ser ou até mesmo caracterizar um abuso e não só uma propaganda indevida", acrescenta o ex-juiz do Tribunal Regional Eleitoral.

O que fazer diante de um assédio eleitoral

Para o trabalhador, uma das principais dificuldades é reconhecer quando uma situação ultrapassou o limite. A pressão nem sempre aparece de forma direta, como uma ameaça explícita.

Nesses casos, é importante guardar registros como mensagens, áudios, vídeos, fotos, convocações e informações sobre possíveis testemunhas que possam ajudar na apuração dos fatos, segundo o MPT.

O órgão informa ainda que denúncias podem ser feitas pela internet e que quem denuncia pode pedir que sua identidade seja mantida em sigilo.

"O trabalhador pode procurar o seu sindicato, pode fazer uma denúncia no Ministério Público do Trabalho. As provas são diversas: podem ser conversas tratadas no WhatsApp, bilhetes, pode ser a própria propaganda eleitoral, uma convocação para reuniões. Vai depender da situação específica", explica Lima.

articles.title: Crise no STF se arrasta por quase um mês e chega ao TSE às vésperas do 1º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Embate que começou restrito a André Mendonça e Alexandre de Moraes atraiu outros ministros da Corte e avançou sobre pautas com impacto eleitoral.
articles.summary: Embate que começou restrito a André Mendonça e Alexandre de Moraes atraiu outros ministros da Corte e avançou sobre pautas com impacto eleitoral.
articles.body:
A crise institucional instalada no Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) está prestes a completar um mês produzindo desgastes internos em várias frentes. Agora, ela também corre o risco de ter impactos no Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), na reta final do primeiro turno.

O grupo de Mendonça espera que a decisão possa ser levada ao plenário já nas sessões desta semana, quarta-feira (30) ou quinta-feira (1), e avaliam ter seis votos para restabelecer a retirada dos posts como determinado pelo TSE.

A ala aposta no apoio de Fachin e Cármen Lúcia. Em outra frente, aliados de Moraes indicam que uma discussão na véspera da eleição pode expor ainda mais o tribunal e acirrar a erosão interna na cúpula do Judiciário.

Flávio Dino, André Mendonça, Alexande de Moraes, Dias Toffoli e Gilmar Mendes — Foto: Alejandro Zambrana/STF

Nesse mês, a crise que surgiu com o embate direto entre André Mendonça e Alexandre de Moraes suplantou as investigações do Caso Master, as mensagens de Daniel Vorcaro e envolveu outros ministros da Corte para uma “guerra” de decisões sobre temas com impacto eleitoral.

Luiz Fux, Dias Toffoli e Nunes Marques se alinharam a Mendonça. Gilmar Mendes, Cristiano Zanin e Flávio Dino ficaram com Moraes. Cármen Lúcia e Fachin são considerados mais independentes, mas nos cálculos internos estariam mais próximos da ala de Mendonça.

Nos dias seguintes à sessão que começou a analisar o relatório da PF, os ministros começaram a divergir em outros temas, chegando a contrariar as decisões tomadas individualmente por colegas.

Gilmar Mendes e André Mendonça — Foto: Rosinei Coutinho/STF

A crise chegou também à discussão sobre precatórios do setor sucroalcooleiro.

Vorcaro se refere a Newton e Camila como “turma do KN”, uma referência a Kassio Nunes Marques, segundo as investigações.

O escritório em que Camila atua fechou um contrato para receber honorários advocatícios de causas envolvendo precatórios de usinas e que haviam sido comprados pelo Master. Newton Ramos teria votado favoravelmente aos interesses de Camila, sua companheira, e do Banco Master.

A ideia é uniformizar o entendimento sobre a tese que discute a necessidade de perícia individualizada para a comprovação de prejuízos causados pela fixação de preços do extinto Instituto do Açúcar e do Álcool (IAA).

O caso mais recente da crise entre os ministros das duas alas da Corte envolve postagens a respeito de Nossa Senhora Aparecida.

articles.summary: Três candidatos participam de debate na RPC, afiliada da TV Globo, nesta terça-feira (29), a partir das 22h15h, com transmissão ao vivo no g1 Paraná.
articles.body:
A RPC , afiliada da TV Globo, realiza nesta terça-feira (29) o debate entre os candidatos ao governo do Paraná , em Curitiba. A transmissão ao vivo começa a partir das 22h15, após a novela “Quem Ama Cuida” na RPC e no g1 Paraná .

Os candidatos poderão ter embates diretos e vão administrar o próprio tempo de fala livremente. O debate será mediado pela jornalista Helen Anacleto, apresentadora do Boa Noite Paraná.

O objetivo do evento é informar o eleitor, que poderá ver os candidatos frente a frente para aprofundar propostas e defender posicionamentos.

Candidatos ao governo do Paraná — Foto: Três candidatos ao governo do Paraná foram convidados para debate - Fotos: Orlando Kissner/Alep | Agência Senado | Carlos Moura/Agência Senado

Como prevê a legislação eleitoral, a RPC convidou os três candidatos com representatividade mínima no Congresso Nacional. São eles:

Como será o debate com candidatos ao governo do Paraná na RPC

O debate da RPC será dividido em quatro blocos, sendo os três primeiros de tema livre e o último bloco será dedicado às considerações finais dos candidatos. Cada candidato terá três minutos para considerações finais.

Em cada bloco de perguntas, cada candidato terá direito a formular uma pergunta e deverá responder uma vez, de forma que todos os candidatos perguntem e respondam.

As regras do debate foram apresentadas pela direção de jornalismo e departamento jurídico da emissora em 22 de setembro aos representantes dos três candidatos, que aprovaram os critérios.

O debate começa às 22h15 na RPC , afiliada da TV Globo no Paraná, com transmissão ao vivo pelo g1 Paraná.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: posso votar em candidato de outro estado? | G1
articles.standfirst: Nas eleições gerais, a regra varia conforme o cargo: presidente pode ser escolhido em todo o país, enquanto governador e parlamentares são votados dentro de cada estado.
articles.summary: Nas eleições gerais, a regra varia conforme o cargo: presidente pode ser escolhido em todo o país, enquanto governador e parlamentares são votados dentro de cada estado.
articles.body:
Nas eleições de 2026, o eleitor não pode votar em candidatos a governador, senador ou deputado que disputem a eleição por outro estado . Para esses cargos, a escolha fica restrita aos candidatos que concorrem pelo estado onde o eleitor tem domicílio eleitoral. Já para presidente, é possível votar em qualquer candidato do país.

Governador, senador, deputado federal e deputado estadual: o eleitor pode votar em qualquer candidato que concorra pelo seu estado, independentemente da cidade.

Presidente: o eleitor pode votar em qualquer candidato do país, independentemente do estado.

Exemplo: um eleitor do Paraná pode votar em um candidato a deputado federal que concorra pelo Paraná, seja ele de Curitiba, Londrina ou qualquer outra cidade paranaense. Mas não pode votar em um candidato que concorra por Santa Catarina.

E se eu estiver em outra cidade no dia da eleição?

É possível votar fora da cidade onde o eleitor tem seu título por meio do voto em trânsito , desde que a pessoa tenha feito a solicitação dentro do prazo estabelecido pela Justiça Eleitoral.

Quem estiver em outra cidade do mesmo estado poderá votar para presidente, governador, senador, deputado federal e deputado estadual ou distrital.

Já quem estiver em outro estado poderá votar somente para presidente.

articles.title: VÍDEO: como os partidos recebem recursos? | G1
articles.standfirst: Entenda como funciona a distribuição do fundo eleitoral, por que o número de deputados e senadores eleitos pesa na divisão dos recursos e de onde vem o dinheiro usado nas campanhas. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Entenda como funciona a distribuição do fundo eleitoral, por que o número de deputados e senadores eleitos pesa na divisão dos recursos e de onde vem o dinheiro usado nas campanhas. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.body:
Você sabia que, no Brasil, empresas não podem financiar campanhas?

Para compensar essa mudança, foi criado o fundo eleitoral , o fundão, que nada mais é que uma cota paga com dinheiro público apenas em ano de disputa eleitoral. A fatia que cada partido vai receber, já foi definida lá atrás, nas eleições de 2022. Então, quanto mais deputados um partido eleger, mais dinheiro ele vai ter para investir na campanha seguinte.

Uma pequena parte desse dinheiro é dividida igualmente entre todos os partidos. Mas o que muda completamente o jogo aqui é a quantidade de deputados e senadores eleitos.

2% distribuídos igualmente entre todas as legendas registradas;

35% conforme a votação obtida para a Câmara dos Deputados;

48% de acordo com o número de deputados federais eleitos (incluindo efeitos de fusões e incorporações);

15% conforme a representação no Senado Federal.

📍 Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

Um total de quase R$ 5 bilhões foi dividido por 30 partidos. Esse valor sai do orçamento do governo federal, é sugerido pela Presidência da República e votado pelo Congresso. Nesta ordem, PL, PT, União Brasil, PSD, PP e MDB vão receber a partir de R$ 400 milhões. O que acompanha o tamanho das bancadas que cada um deles formou em 2022.

PL : R$ 881,6 milhões. A parcela destinada ao PL neste ano triplicou na comparação com 2022, quando o partido recebeu R$ 268,1 milhões;

PT : R$ 615,3 milhões- 12,4% do total. O valor é 23% superior ao recebido em 2022, quando o partido teve acesso a R$ 499,6 milhões;

Existe ainda outro tipo de recurso: o fundo partidário. Esse é o dinheiro que mantém a estrutura do partido funcionando. Ele serve para pagar funcionários, aluguel da sede, contas de água e luz.

A maior parte desse dinheiro também é distribuída conforme o desempenho das siglas. Mas há uma regra para participar dessa divisão, um percentual mínimo de votos que a legenda precisa receber para ter direito ao recurso.

Quem não atinge esse desempenho mínimo — a chamada cláusula de barreira — perde acesso ao fundo partidário e também ao direito de participar da propaganda gratuita no rádio e na televisão. Agora não existem mais as coligações.

➡️ Cláusula de barreira: 3% de votos para a Câmara dos Deputados distribuídos nacionalmente ou eleger pelo menos 15 deputados federais.

O fundo partidário é diferente do fundão porque é pago mensalmente aos partidos, todos os anos, independentemente da eleição. Com esses valores, os partidos podem ainda pagar conteúdos na internet, passagens aéreas para não filiados, e contratação de advogados e contadores. Esse dinheiro vem do orçamento federal, de doações e multas eleitorais.

No primeiro semestre de 2026, uma média de 103,5 milhões foram distribuídos por mês para 19 partidos- R$ 5,5 milhões para cada legenda.

Existe ainda uma terceira fonte de recursos: a vaquinha virtual.

Nesta modalidade, válida desde 2018, pessoas físicas, podem doar para as campanhas por meio de sites cadastrados na Justiça Eleitoral. Há um limite de doação individual de acordo com a renda do doador.

Resumindo: o fundo partidário mantém a estrutura do partido funcionando o ano inteiro; o fundo eleitoral ajuda a financiar a disputa para as eleições; e a vaquinha virtual permite que os eleitores apoiem diretamente as siglas.

articles.title: Russell Brand to moderate panel at MAHA summit
articles.summary: Comedian Russell Brand on Tuesday will moderate one of the panels scheduled for the second Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) summit in Washington, D.C. Brand, who has been part of and supported the MAHA movement launched by Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., is set to moderate a discussion about reforms…
articles.body:
Comedian Russell Brand on Tuesday will moderate one of the panels scheduled for the second Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) summit in Washington, D.C.

Brand, who has been part of and supported the MAHA movement launched by Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., is set to moderate a discussion about reforms to the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).

The comedian is one of the few celebrities to speak at the summit. Former boxing heavyweight champion Mike Tyson will be part of a panel discussion on the “MAHA athlete.” “Curb Your Enthusiasm” star Cheryl Hines, Kennedy’s wife, will give an “exciting announcement” before Kennedy holds a “fireside chat” with Vice President Vance to close out the event.

Brand’s attendance comes before he is expected to go to trial in London next month. He has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault — all in connection with allegations made by six women about incidents that took place between 1999 and 2009, The Hollywood Reporter wrote in March.

Brand was granted conditional bail during a court appearance in May 2025.

The trial was initially set to start in June before Justice Joel Bennathan announced that it was delayed, Sky News reported. The outlet added that the trial is expected to last two months.

London’s Metropolitan Police began investigating Brand in September 2023 after several women came forward following the release of an installment of “Dispatches” on Channel 4, where a woman told filmmakers that she was in a relationship with Brand when she was 16 and he was 31. She alleged that the now 51-year-old comedian was “emotionally abusive and controlling.”

Police said Brand allegedly raped one woman in the Bournemouth area in 1999, indecently assaulted a woman in 2001 in London’s Westminster area, orally raped and sexually assaulted a woman in 2004, and sexually assaulted a woman between 2004 and 2005.

Another woman accused Brand of raping her in his Los Angeles home in 2012, according to an investigative report in The Sunday Times.

Brand denied the charges in April 2025. He said in a video on social media that he was “a fool before I lived in the light of the lord.”

“I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile,” he added. “But what I never was, was a rapist. I’ve never engaged in nonconsensual activity. I pray that you can see that by looking in my eyes.”

A year later in April 2026, Brand admitted in an interview with Megyn Kelly on her YouTube show that he had “exploitative” consensual sex with a 16-year-old girl when he was 30. He noted that the United Kingdom’s age of consent is 16, whereas it is 18 in the U.S., and said he was “a very different person” and “immature” at the time.

“It is exploitative,” he said. “Consensual sex with a lot of people, when there is a strong power differential, as there is when you are a famous man who has the ability to attract women that I had at that time, I think involves exploitation.”

articles.title: ABC's 'The View' co-host Ana Navarro urges viewers to vote for Dem in key Florida congressional race
articles.summary: "The View" co-host Ana Navarro urged viewers to vote for Florida Democrat Eliott Rodriguez, sparking accusations of electioneering against ABC.
articles.body: ABC is facing blowback Monday after "The View" co-host Ana Navarro urged viewers to vote for a Democrat in a key Florida congressional race. Navarro marveled at the tightening race between incumbent Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., and her Democratic opponent Eliott Rodriguez in the Sunshine State's 27th district. Salazar recently made headlines for releasing an ad critical of President Donald Trump's immigration policies. The host noted to viewers she lives in that district. ABC FIRES BACK AT FCC PROBE OF 'THE VIEW,' CALLS OUT AGENCY'S 'CHILLING EFFECT ON FIRST AMENDMENT' "I had taken for granted this race because she won two years ago by 20 points. And this is a district Donald Trump won by 15 points ... but polls have her dead even," Navarro said. "So, anybody who lives in Coral Gables, in Miami, in Key Biscayne, in downtown Miami, pay attention to that race and go vote because it's going to matter," she continued. articles.title: Senate defeats proposal to limit ticket price increases for college sports
articles.summary: The Senate voted Monday evening to defeat an amendment sponsored by Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) to cap ticket price increases for college sporting events to four percent a year, even as ticket prices for some marquee games have soared in recent years. Kennedy proposed his amendment to the Protect College Sports Act, a sweeping bill…
articles.body:
The Senate voted Monday evening to defeat an amendment sponsored by Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) to cap ticket price increases for college sporting events to four percent a year, even as ticket prices for some marquee games have soared in recent years.

Kennedy proposed his amendment to the Protect College Sports Act, a sweeping bill that would overhaul compensation, recruitment and eligibility rules for college athletes.

Kennedy argued that the bill would be a windfall for college athletic programs and coaches but would likely leave fans paying ever-rising prices for big-time college football and basketball games.

“Who makes college athletics possible? Who generates all of this cash flow? The fans. And we’ve done nothing for them. Zero,” Kennedy declared on the Senate floor before the vote.

“The ticket prices keep going up and every single person in this body has been all across America talking about affordability, and sometimes the prices go up 30 percent to 40 percent,” he said.

Kennedy proposed capping the increase in ticket prices for college sporting events to four percent a year.

The amendment failed by a vote of 42 to 54. It needed 60 votes to be adopted.

Axios reported earlier this year that average college football ticket prices have increased from $59 in 2015 to $129 in 2025.

Sports Illustrated reported that the cost of game-day football experiences at the University of Texas have soared by more than 45 percent compared to last year while game-day prices increased at University of Tennessee increased by more than 60 percent compared to last year.

The average ticket price for a Big Ten college football game was $73 in 2024 and the average price for Northwestern University games was $225, according to the Daily Iowan.

Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) spoke in opposition to Kennedy’s proposal.

“I oppose it. It would set a price control on sports tickets. It does not distinguish between large and small institutions, applies the same mandate to every university and to every single sport, from the small local community college to the [historically black college or university,]” he said.

Cruz argued that if Kennedy’s amendment were adopted it would “harm schools from being able to respond when market factors change.”

articles.title: Senate passes bipartisan bill to overhaul college sports
articles.summary: President Donald Trump wants the House to clear the measure quickly.
articles.body:
The Senate passed a sweeping bipartisan bill Monday that would overhaul the multibillion-dollar college sports industry — a major legislative victory shared by members of both parties and President Donald Trump, who wants to sign the package as soon as possible.

A high priority for Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz of Texas and the panel's top Democrat, Maria Cantwell of Washington, the Protect College Sports Act would replace a patchwork of state laws governing student athlete compensation, transfers and eligibility with one overarching federal rulebook.

"Today the Senate has the opportunity to protect the half million college athletes and the millions more who follow in their footsteps," said Cruz in a floor speech Monday. "Students are transferring three or four times. Pros are trying to play ball against college kids. Conflicting court decisions have created a fragmented system — one that no one intended. And young men and women are losing opportunities to compete and receive an education."

But while the 77-22 vote would ordinarily present itself as a welcome glimpse of cross-party unity, it is now being overshadowed by a murky outlook in the House, where Republicans oppose multiple provisions of the Senate package.

Democrats, meanwhile, are smarting from a highly-charged debate over whether the legislation would exploit college athletes of color — and some are questioning why their colleagues would split from the AFL-CIO and the NAACP, two organizations core to the party's base that oppose the legislation.

That the vote was one of the last actions senators will take before leaving Washington to campaign for the midterms also has also presented unsavory optics for many Republicans, who are desperate to show they are serious about alleviating concerns around rising gas prices and interest rates.

"Is this really what we should be spending our time on?" Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), one of the most vocal opponents of the legislation, asked Monday night on the Senate floor. "Our country faces real challenges. Gas is at $5. Diesel costs are a record high. We're at war abroad. Health care expenses are skyrocketing."

"And," Booker continued, "the United States Senate is spending precious time rewriting the rules of college sports while athletes' groups, survivors of sexual assault, labor, civil rights leaders are all begging Congress to slow down and listen to their voices. What does this say about our priorities?"

In one apparent acknowledgement of the dynamics at play, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) offered an amendment that would have put limits on how much schools and conferences can increase the price of tickets for games — arguing it would help keep costs stable for fans amid a nationwide affordability crisis. Cruz objected to the proposal, arguing it would "harm schools from being able to respond when market factors change."

Kennedy's amendment was ultimately rejected, while senators adopted a change to the bill sought by Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) to require the disclosure of foreign financing of intercollegiate athletics.

Cruz in a Senate floor speech Monday presented the Protect College Sports Act as a binary choice for his colleagues: Stand by, or turn their backs, on student athletes who are currently being undercut by bidding wars that force schools to scrap programs because they don't make headlines or big time television contracts.

Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), one of the bill's biggest champions, said the legislation was necessary to protect "a uniquely American institution" that has, in recent years, "come to be defined by increasing financial and regulatory instability that have thrown the entire system into jeopardy."

And Cantwell has insisted the bill is a win for the half-million college athletes across the country — particularly women and participants in Olympic sports programs — who are losing out on money and resources as big-ticket departments like football spend big money to attract top talent.

"We need to stop stealing money out of college [and] university institutions for education, for tuition, for professors, and putting it into an arms race on sports," she said Monday.

All these arguments are lost on members of the Congressional Black Caucus, of which Booker is a part — with its chair, Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), saying in an interview last week the bill fails to "center the lives of the athletes."

"There's so much that this bill neglects," she said, pointing specifically to health care provisions.

The all-Democratic CBC has been unanimously opposed to moving forward on any college sports bill since May, following the late April Supreme Court decision that allowed Republican-led states to eliminate majority-minority districts across the South.

In a statement at the time, the CBC said it would not support legislation "benefiting major athletic institutions that continue to remain silent while Black voting rights and Black political power are being systematically dismantled."

Some Democrats in the Senate also lamented that the bill would set student athletes back after many have benefited from various federal court rulings entitling them to compensation for their name, image and likeness.

"This bill…only caps the money going to the players — does nothing to cap the money going to the coaches," Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said on the floor Monday.

On the Republican side of the aisle, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise — who was heavily involved in working on a House version of a college sports overhaul bill that has repeatedly fallen short of support — has consistently raised concerns that the Senate measure would leave the door open to possible unionization efforts by players.

House conservatives are also expected to oppose provisions in the Senate bill that would provide $1 billion for competitive grants to Historically Black Colleges and Universities without offsets; could increase litigation related to student unionization efforts; provide no cap on granting international student scholarships; and generally insert Congress into the business of college sports.

GOP Rep. Michael Baumgartner of Washington, who introduced an earlier House version of the bill, posted on social media Monday that the bill will "have a better than 50% chance in the House." He also said that even with the president's blessing, the legislation will need Democratic votes, pointing out the "Dem CBC will be a factor."

But Republicans may ultimately face pressure to fall in line: Trump promoted the Senate bill as recently as this weekend in an interview with Clay Travis, founder of the digital sports column Sport & State.

Trump also suggested Speaker Mike Johnson might bring the House back into session before the midterms to clear the measure for his signature.

"We have to get it voted on," he told Travis, "and we're counting on the House — and I think the House will come through, too."

Speaking with reporters following the final passage vote late Monday night, Cruz said his "hope" is that Johnson calls House members back to Washington to vote on the bill.

"The House can pass it a single day and put it on the president's desk. President Trump is eager to sign this legislation," he said.

When asked when he last spoke to Johnson, however, Cruz admitted it had been about two weeks.

"At the end of the day, it is the speaker's decision," he added. "But I had a very positive and lengthy conversation with the speaker about doing so. I hope he will do so, and I think that that would be a win-win for everyone."

Riley Rogerson contributed to this report.

articles.title: Senate passes ‘Protect College Sports Act’ with sweeping bipartisan vote
articles.summary: The Senate on Monday passed a landmark piece of legislation that aims to address growing concerns about fairness and equity in college sports, bolstering the National Collegiate Athletic Association’s (NCAA) power to enforce its rules and potentially reshaping the future of collegiate athletics for years to come. The “Protect College Sports Act” (PCSA), a bill championed…
articles.body:
The Senate on Monday passed a landmark piece of legislation that aims to address growing concerns about fairness and equity in college sports, bolstering the National Collegiate Athletic Association’s (NCAA) power to enforce its rules and potentially reshaping the future of collegiate athletics for years to come.

The “Protect College Sports Act” (PCSA), a bill championed by Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), cleared the upper chamber 77-22 after months of tense bipartisan negotiations and vocal pushback from critics of the NCAA and senators in both parties.

The bill, among its top priorities, hands the NCAA sweeping federal antitrust protection shielding it from lawsuits around the enforcement of its rules and caps the amount of money student athletes can be paid for their name, image and likeness.

It limits agent fees at 5 percent and school spending on athletes at $50 million annually. It guarantees scholarships for 10 years after eligibility, as well, while allowing athletes to transfer once without having to sit out a year.

The bill also sets guidelines on conference realignment and seeks to enforce minimum revenue sharing standards at major colleges where football and men’s basketball earn schools millions each year, while smaller sports are under growing financial pressure.

“It would be nice if college sports could somehow magically fix itself, but this is a matter of law, federal law, and only Congress can fix it,” Cruz said during a recent floor speech promoting the bill. “Now I know some argue that college sports are doing just fine. They point to high television ratings, enthusiastic fan bases, and packed stadiums. But popularity does not demonstrate that the system is healthy. It simply proves that the system is worth saving. “

Monday’s vote was the culmination of months of work by a bipartisan group of Senators, led by Cruz and Cantwell, to win over skeptical Democrats, who raised concern the bill would disproportionately harm minority athletes’ earning potential and hand the NCAA and top member schools too much power.

Several labor groups, the NAACP and the Congressional Black Caucus have come out against the bill and vowed to fight it in the House, where it is expected to be considered when lawmakers return to Washington, D.C., after the midterm elections.

Among the bill’s top critics in the Senate were Cory Booker (D-NJ), who played football at Stanford University and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), who argued the bill would essentially “preserve the exploitative model of college sports.”

“This is a bill not about student athletes, it’s about wealthy coaches and wealthy institutions and an NCAA who has enjoyed unbridled power for decades as we watch discrimination and hardships [of student athletes],” Booker said during floor speech on Monday that blasted the bill. “And finally the athletes were getting some power … and this body rushes in to say we’re protecting college athletes. Well that is not true.”

Monday’s final vote came after lawmakers voted down a handful of amendments to the sweeping bill, including a provision introduced by Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) limiting increases to ticket prices schools can charge for major sporting events and a measure that would have capped coach salaries, introduced by Booker.

The PCSA’s passage marks a major achievement for the NCAA on Capitol Hill, where it has spent millions lobbying lawmakers and rolling out an aggressive advertising campaign advocating federal intervention in its rulemaking and enforcement in recent months.

In a statement on Monday evening, NCAA President Charlie Baker thanked Senators for their work on the bill and said “there is much work left to do” in the House “to ensure student-athlete benefits are codified into federal law and future generations of young people can access those benefits and use college sports as the launching point for their careers.”

A key moment for the legislation came in August when the SEC and Big Ten, the top two conference in college athletics, endorsed the bill, saying it was necessary to preserve competitive balance and put an end to the constant litigation schools face in regard to issues like the transfer portal and eligibility.

The measure passed out of the Senate Commerce Committee in June with a bipartisan vote and notched its first major legislative victory earlier this month when it cleared a procedural vote , with more than 70 votes for, despite pushback from senators in both parties.

Several conservative members held out on the legislation over concerns about how it would impact state laws on funding for transgender athletes in sports, while a pair of Florida lawmakers raised issue with its provisions regarding conference realignment standards.

The bill has been endorsed by President Trump , who earlier this year set up a task force on college sports that includes major figures like former University of Alabama coach Nick Saban and New York Yankees President Randy Levine.

After the PCSA passed its first procedural vote earlier this month, Trump in a Truth Social post called it “great news” that Congress was “straightening out the horrible situation taking place with respect to College Sports.”

“It is out of control, and will lead to bankruptcies and disaster for many Colleges,” the president said. “If nothing is done, it is also very bad for Women’s Sports, all Olympic Sports, and everything else other than Football — But even Football is bad because, without ‘caps,’ all Colleges will be financially consumed and, in many cases, it will ruin them.”

The bill is expected to face an uphill battle in the House after the midterm elections, where other similar efforts to regulate the big business of college sports have faltered.

The “SCORE Act,” a GOP-led measure that would have created similar federal standards and protected the NCAA, died this summer in the House after the Congressional Black Caucus held out support.

Cruz, who appeared on ESPN’s “College Gameday” earlier this month to advocate for the bill, has repeatedly suggested the House should make the PCSA a priority in the coming session and went so far as to say Trump should sign the bill live on the popular college football pregame show.

“We’ve gotta get there first,” Cruz told reporters the day before the Senate’s first vote on a bill he has been spearheading for months. “But it would be an amazing victory for student athletes if we can get that done.”

articles.title: Georgia Gov. Kemp suspends state gas tax for 30 days
articles.summary: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) on Monday signed an executive order suspending the state’s gas tax for 30 days as the Iran war sends gas prices soaring. The order, which starts at 12:01 a.m. EDT Tuesday, suspends Georgia’s motor fuel excise tax of 33.3 cents per gallon for gasoline and 37.3 cents per gallon for…
articles.body:
Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp (R) on Monday signed an executive order suspending the state’s gas tax for 30 days as the Iran war sends gas prices soaring .

The order, which starts at 12:01 a.m. EDT Tuesday, suspends Georgia’s motor fuel excise tax of 33.3 cents per gallon for gasoline and 37.3 cents per gallon for diesel. The suspension could cost the state about $200 million a month, though Kemp could offset this by using the state’s surplus, the Atlanta-Journal Constitution reported .

Kemp’s order also suspends weight restrictions on commercial vehicles to reduce the cost of transporting goods.

The governor said in a statement that the state government has been “able to give billions of dollars in relief to hardworking Georgians.” Kemp previously suspended the Peach State’s gas tax in March, an order that carried on through Memorial Day.

“We’ve remained committed to helping them and our small businesses fight through the tough times, and that’s why I’m taking this action today to give further relief,” he added.

The order received support from Lt. Gov. Burt Jones (R), state House Speaker Jon Burns (R) and Georgia Department of Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper.

“This announcement means immediate relief for Georgia families struggling to afford gas and groceries and Georgia farmers facing diesel prices that have more than doubled in recent weeks,” Harper said in Kemp’s statement. “We have been working closely with Gov. Kemp’s office to make this happen, and I am grateful that we have a governor who is willing to take action to give hardworking Georgians relief when fuel prices spike.”

Georgia’s average gas price sits at $4.19, almost 30 cents less than the national average. The state’s average last year was $2.88, according to AAA . Diesel in Georgia, at $6.35, is about 20 cents less than the national average.

Gas and diesel prices have skyrocketed over the past seven months since the start of the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran. The Iranian government shut down the Strait of Hormuz, where around 20 percent of the world’s oil is exported, leading to a rise in prices.

These increases have hit Americans at home, already concerned about the cost of living after years of inflation. Sixty percent of respondents to Emerson College’s poll last week said President Trump’s economic policies are making the economy worse.

The president has dismissed concerns over the rising gas prices for several months, though he released 172 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March. The stockpile hit below 300 million barrels of oil , the lowest it has been since 1982.

At a rally for GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley in North Carolina earlier this month, Trump said prices will go “ tumbling down ” after the conflict ends, “like rocket ships in reverse.”

“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done,” he said. “Remember that. It’s a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more.”

articles.body:
Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and his Democratic opponent, Cait Conley, clashed during a televised midterm debate Monday night, sparring over a range of issues including affordability, housing and foreign policy.

The News 12 debate featured questions from voters as well as the outlet’s senior political reporter Tara Rosenblum. Lawler largely touted his congressional record and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Republicans have branded as the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, while Conley focused on what she would prioritize if elected to Congress.

The debate, however, grew heated over a question on U.S. aid to Israel. Asked whether American taxpayers should continue funding Israel even if it tries to phase off of assistance, Lawler argued the aid remains in U.S. interest, particularly for American troops in the region.

“They have not committed a genocide. Let’s be very clear about that,” Lawler said, accusing some Democrats of wavering in their support for Israel because of what he called the “radical antisemitic base of support within their party.”

Lawler also invoked New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), saying, “I don’t respect his position on Israel. I don’t respect where the Democratic Party is going when it comes to supporting our greatest ally in the region.”

In response, Conley said she condemns antisemitism happening “within both political parties,” prompting Lawler to repeatedly ask her whether she supports Mamdani. At one point, Conley threw the question back at Lawler by asking whether he’s denounced President Trump and claiming that he votes with Trump 100 percent of the time.

“I have not voted with Donald Trump 100 percent of the time. What I’ve done is actually do my job, which is to represent my constituents and actually work in a bipartisan way. Why do you think Jared Golden, a Democrat from Maine, endorsed me? My best friend in Congress is Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat. We work collaboratively all the time… How are you going to engage in bipartisanship when you call Republicans the greatest threat to America?” Lawler responded.

The two also challenged each other over tariffs, with Conley attacking the Trump administration’s decision to implement them and Lawler’s support of the move. Conley argued that the administration has been “absolutely reckless in the administration of foreign tariffs that have jacked up prices on goods for the average household in the Hudson Valley by $4,200.”

“That means families in the Hudson Valley are paying $4,200 more today than they were before the tariffs. We are literally paying the harm of votes like Mike Lawler’s eight times in support of those tariffs, and families deserve better,” Conley said.

Lawler, meanwhile, said that he thinks “tariffs as a tool to force fair trade is critical.”

“When you look at Europe, for instance, and the American taxpayers subsidizing European prescription drug prices, tariffs actually forced change and brought down prescription drug prices by over 3 percent, the largest decline in 60 years,” Lawler said. “That was a positive thing, forcing China, a very bad actor when it comes to trade policy, to change its ways and actually invest in the United States is important.”

Lawler’s seat is rated as a toss up by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.
